title: Without fear
hookLine: with no walls around the mind, there is no fear

cards: A message sits unsent on the screen: an apology, or a no, put off for a week. The heart is loud. The hands are a little cold.
Nothing in that message can hurt anyone. So what is the fear about? Look closer and there's often a wall being guarded.
I'm the one who's never wrong. I'm the one who never lets people down. The fear stands at the wall like a guard at a gate, and the bigger the wall, the more guards it needs.
Today's line from the Heart Sutra is only a few words long. With no walls, no fear.

teach.b: Because there was nothing to attain, the bodhisattva relied on wisdom. The sutra goes on: so the mind has no walls. And because there are no walls, there is no fear.
Far beyond upside-down views, the bodhisattva reaches nirvana.
The Sanskrit for walls is cittāvaraṇa. Citta, the mind. Āvaraṇa, a covering, an obstruction, something that closes in. In Xuanzang's Chinese, the word suggests being caught or snagged.
Buddhist teachers say they're built from those upside-down views.
The classic list has four: taking what changes for permanent, what can't satisfy for lasting happiness, what has no fixed self for a self, and what is unlovely for beautiful.

Each wall is an idea about yourself and the world, held as if it were solid. Fear guards it. When wisdom sees that the wall is made of conditions, like everything else in this sutra, the guard has less to do.
Two honest limits. First, the sutra is describing the bodhisattva, someone deep in wisdom. It doesn't promise that one reading switches fear off.
Second, nothing here says to ignore real danger. The flinch that pulls your hand from a hot stove isn't a wall; it's your body doing its job.
The fear the sutra points at is the kind that guards an idea.
Name the wall, and very often the fear gets smaller, not because you fought it, but because you saw what it was protecting.

how: The Heart Sutra is often chanted at Mahayana funerals, memorial services and bedsides, and many practitioners recite it when they're afraid, drawing on its line about a mind without walls.

o: no walls in the mind for fear to guard
bravely ignoring every danger you face

games.q: match each piece of today's line.
p: what the walls are built from

s: the Heart Sutra promises that one reading switches fear off
it describes the bodhisattva, someone deep in wisdom; it's a direction, not a switch.
the classic list of upside-down views has four
permanence, happiness, self and beauty, each seen where it isn't.
the sutra says to ignore real danger
the fear it points at guards an idea, not the flinch from a hot stove.

games.q: you've put off sending a hard message for a week and your heart pounds every time you open it. what does today's teaching suggest trying first?
o: name the idea about yourself the fear is guarding.
delete the message so the wall stays safe.
games.why: the sutra links fear to walls around the mind; naming the wall is the first step to seeing it's made of conditions.

practice: Let one small fear come to mind, a manageable one, not the biggest, and notice where it lives in the body: the chest, the stomach, the throat.

Then ask quietly what wall it's guarding, what idea about you would crumble if it happened, and just name it. You don't have to knock it down; let the breath move around it, like air around a fence post.

wordCard.voice: Without fear. In the Heart Sutra, a mind with no walls around it has nothing for fear to guard.

orig.note: Sanskrit cittāvaraṇa: a covering or obstruction of the mind; the Heart Sutra says without it there is no fear.

carryVoice: Your line: no walls, no fear. Fewer walls, and fewer guards. Day two hundred seventy-four.
